text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Special tax police will be hired from next year to more effectively combat tax fraud following an investigation on how to battle economic crimes.

- A Bosnian delegation will soon visit Sweden to help discuss the support for the return of Bosnian refugees to their homes. Prime Minister Goran Persson, on a visit to Bosnia, warns municipalities not to set up too many ambitious solutions about returning refugees.

- Prime Minister Goran Persson turned against Swedish chief executives who wrote a column criticising the government, particularly its desicion to start phasing out nuclear power. "There will be a big tug of war about the good things in life and these people have already helped themselves," Persson said.

- Construction group Skanska has more capital than it needs to run its business and said it will transfer eight to 10 billion crowns to its shareholders. The group posted a 1996 profit of 5.17 billion crowns after financial items compared to 2.57 billion in 1995.
- NCC meanwhile posted a 1996 profit after financial items of 462 million crowns compared to 230 million in 1995, but the company painted a gloomy picture of the Swedish construction industry.
- Volvo Aero's decision to close its operations in Arboga, Sweden was an economically justified move, a report by a consulting group showed.

- Metals and mining group Trelleborg has opened its wallet finally, buying North American company Yale-South Haven Inc that has an annual turnover of about one billion crowns. More deals are on the way, said Trelleborg managing director Kjell Nilsson.

- Rolling bearing manufacturer SKF said it would set up new joint ventures in China in both bearing and seals. SKF managing director Peter Augustsson said the deals show SKF's aspirations to become the market leader in China. "We are expecting to see a pronounced upswing in manufacturing and sales in China," the newspaper quotes him as saying.
- The Czech Republic, Hungary and Estonia may become the new tiger economies of Europe, said Jannik Lindbaek, head of the International Finance Corporation during a visit to Stockholm.

- Norway's Schibsted media group is aggressively challenging Sweden's Bonnier group on its domestic market. Schibsted and Sandrews, which operates a chain of cinemas in Sweden, will hold a news conference today to announce an expansion of their cooperation.

- The first tourist campaign targeting German skiers produced a positive result. Ski resorts Salen and Idre reported visits from 30 to 40 percent more German tourists this winter compared to a year earlier.
